title: 2 Samuel 3:22–30
context: Joab returns from a raid with plunder and learns that Abner has come and gone in peace. He confronts David, accusing Abner of coming only to deceive and spy on him. Without David’s knowledge, Joab sends messengers to bring Abner back from the well of Sirah, takes him aside in the gate of Hebron as if to speak privately, and strikes him dead in revenge for his brother Asahel, whom Abner had killed in battle. When David hears of it, he declares himself and his kingdom guiltless of Abner’s blood and pronounces a heavy curse on Joab’s house. The narrator closes by naming Joab and Abishai as the killers. Both traditions read the passage soberly as an account of private vengeance that threatened David’s reign and that David publicly disowned.

verses.text: Behold, David’s servants and Joab came from a raid and brought in a great plunder with them; but Abner was not with David in Hebron, for he had sent him away, and he had gone in peace.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the narrator repeats that Abner had gone in peace, timing Joab’s return just after his departure. The repetition emphasizes David’s peaceful intent and sets up the tension between David’s policy and Joab’s personal agenda, which will lead to tragedy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise observe the narrator’s careful timing and repetition, which establish David’s innocence before the violence happens. Both traditions agree that the text is concerned to show that David did not plot against Abner, which becomes important for how Israel views David’s reign.

verses.text: When Joab and all the army who was with him had come, they told Joab, “Abner the son of Ner came to the king, and he has sent him away, and he has gone in peace.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers point out that Joab’s men inform him that Abner came to the king and was sent away in peace. The report reaches Joab as news he did not expect, and his reaction shows how his own loyalties and grievances shape his response to David’s policy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the threefold mention of peace across these verses underlines the agreement David had made. Both traditions see Joab entering a situation already settled by the king, which he will overturn by his own initiative and violence.

verses.text: Then Joab came to the king and said, “What have you done? Behold, Abner came to you. Why is it that you have sent him away, and he is already gone?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that Joab confronts David bluntly, questioning why he let Abner go. Joab speaks to the king with surprising boldness, which suggests the degree of power he holds as commander and his willingness to challenge David when he thinks David has erred.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note Joab’s blunt challenge to the king and the strained relationship it reveals. Both traditions agree that the narrative is showing the difficulty David has controlling the sons of Zeruiah, a theme David will lament at the end of the chapter.

verses.text: You know Abner the son of Ner. He came to deceive you, and to know your going out and your coming in, and to know all that you do.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Joab accuses Abner of coming to deceive David and to learn his movements. The accusation may reflect genuine suspicion, but it also serves Joab’s own desire for revenge and perhaps his concern for his position as commander, though the text does not state the latter.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Joab casts suspicion on Abner, whether sincerely or as a pretext. Both traditions agree that the narrator does not endorse Joab’s view, since the preceding verses present Abner’s alliance as genuine, and both see suspicion here becoming a cover for violence.

verses.text: When Joab had come out from David, he sent messengers after Abner, and they brought him back from the well of Sirah; but David didn’t know it.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers point out that Joab sends messengers after Abner and brings him back from the well of Sirah, while David did not know it. The note that David did not know is central: it places responsibility for what follows on Joab, not on the king. The location of the well of Sirah is not certain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise stress that David did not know of Joab’s action, which clears David of complicity. Both traditions agree that the narrator wants readers to see that Abner’s death was not David’s policy, and that Joab acted on his own authority in secret.

verses.text: When Abner had returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside into the middle of the gate to speak with him quietly, and struck him there in the body, so that he died for the blood of Asahel his brother.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers are struck by Joab taking Abner aside in the gate as if to speak quietly and then striking him in the body. The killing is treacherous, carried out under the appearance of friendship, and the text names the motive plainly: revenge for the blood of Asahel his brother.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the killing takes place in Hebron, and many note that Hebron was already designated a city of refuge (Joshua 20:7), which would make a killing there especially grave, though the text does not draw out that point. Both traditions agree that Joab’s act is murder disguised as conversation, and that it is presented as private vengeance, not lawful justice.

verses.text: Afterward, when David heard it, he said, “I and my kingdom are guiltless before the LORD forever of the blood of Abner the son of Ner.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that David declares himself and his kingdom guiltless before the LORD of Abner’s blood. David publicly separates himself from the murder, which matters both morally and politically, since Israel must not think David had his rival killed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see David’s declaration as both a sincere disavowal and a public necessity. Both traditions agree that shed blood was regarded as a grave matter requiring accountability before God, and David is careful to place the guilt where it belongs.

verses.text: Let it fall on the head of Joab and on all his father’s house. Let there not fail from the house of Joab one who has a discharge, or who is a leper, or who leans on a staff, or who falls by the sword, or who lacks bread.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers point out that David calls down a curse on Joab’s house, naming afflictions such as discharge, leprosy, weakness, violent death, and hunger. David’s words express the seriousness of the crime, though he does not, at this point, bring Joab to justice himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that David entrusts the punishment of Joab to the LORD through this curse rather than acting directly. Both traditions agree that the curse reflects the gravity of innocent blood, and both note that the unresolved matter of Joab’s guilt will return near the end of David’s life (1 Kings 2:5–6).

verses.text: So Joab and Abishai his brother killed Abner, because he had killed their brother Asahel at Gibeon in the battle.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the narrator names both Joab and Abishai as responsible for Abner’s death, giving the reason as revenge for Asahel, whom Abner killed at Gibeon in battle (2 Samuel 2:18–23). The narrator thus distinguishes Abner’s killing of Asahel in battle from this act of private vengeance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise observe the distinction between a death in battle and a calculated murder in peacetime. Both traditions agree that the narrator records the motive without excusing it, and that naming Abishai alongside Joab shows the involvement of both brothers in the plot, even if Joab struck the blow.
